description: Pronominal adverbs built on here-, there- and where- that replace a repeated noun phrase with a single opaque word.
evidence: Words like hereof, thereof, and whereof (and further derivatives, including -at, -in, -after, -before, -with, -by, -above, -on, -upon) are not often used in standard English.
testable: Count tokens matching (here|there|where)(of|to|in|by|under|after|before|with|upon|as|at) and report the count per 1000 words.

description: The modal shall used to impose a legal obligation rather than to mark future time, keeping it productive long after ordinary speech dropped it.
evidence: Shall is, however, still widely used in bureaucratic documents, especially documents written by lawyers.
testable: Count shall and shall not as a share of all modals (shall, must, may, will, should); a shall share above roughly 20 percent marks drafting style.

description: A modal system in which shall and shall not encode mandatory action and prohibition instead of describing the future.
evidence: Legislative acts and contracts sometimes use "shall" and "shall not" to express mandatory action and prohibition.
testable: Tag every modal as obligation, permission or futurity and compute the obligation-to-futurity ratio per document.

description: May and should carry non-mandatory, discretionary meaning, so a detector has to separate permission from obligation.
evidence: "Will" declares intent or simple futurity, and "should" and "may" express nonmandatory provisions.
testable: Count may, is entitled to and is authorized to alongside shall; rights-granting text shows may-dominant modality with few conditions.

description: The same shall can mean must, may or will, which is why plain-language bodies advise dropping the word and why it attracts litigation.
evidence: Owing its use in varying legal contexts, its meaning can be ambiguous; the United States government's Plain Language group advises writers not to use the word at all.
testable: Flag documents where shall takes an inanimate subject, co-occurs with must, or appears in a definition, as candidates for ambiguous use.

description: Fixed old-fashioned adverbs and adverbial phrases survive in legal text where a plain equivalent exists.
evidence: When you’re making word choices, pick the familiar or commonly used word over the unusual or obscure.
testable: Match a closed list (heretofore, herein, herewith, theretofore, hereinbefore, hitherto) and report hits per 1000 words.

description: Two near-synonyms joined by and or or to express one legal concept, a habit inherited from mixed-language drafting.
evidence: The mix of languages used in early legalese led to the tendency in legal English to string together two or three words to convey a single legal concept.
testable: Match a lexicon of known pairs and also count any two coordinated words separated by and/or whose meanings overlap by WordNet similarity.

description: Three or more coordinated near-synonyms chained together, a conjoined phrase that survives because every word is presumed to carry meaning.
evidence: Conjoining words is still extremely common in legal language.
testable: Count runs of three or more comma-and coordinated items inside one clause, excluding list contexts introduced by such as or including.

description: Wordy, repeated formulaic phrasing that fills space without adding meaning.
evidence: Lawyers are very prone to use wordy and redundant phraseology, including what is sometimes called boilerplate.
examples: subject to and in accordance with
testable: Match recurring multi-word formulas across a corpus and score documents by the share of tokens inside repeated n-grams.

description: Verbs are turned into abstract nouns and propped up by a light verb, so the action disappears into a thing.
evidence: A hidden verb (or nominalization) is a verb converted into a noun.
testable: Count nouns in -tion, -ment, -ance, -sion preceded by make, give, effect, conduct, carry out or undertake, plus bare nominalisations of common legal verbs.

description: Passives drop the actor, which hides who must act and lends the text an impersonal, authoritative tone.
evidence: Passive sentences allow the speaker or writer to omit reference to the actor (as in the girl was injured at 5:30).
examples: the parties are deemed to have agreed
testable: Parse be/get plus past participle and compute the proportion with no by-phrase, per 1000 words.

description: Legal sentences run far longer than general prose and stack embedded clauses inside each other.
evidence: Studies show that sentences in legal language are quite a bit longer than in other styles, and also have more embeddings, making them more complex.
testable: Compute mean words per sentence and count subordinators (that, which, provided that, subject to, unless) per sentence; flag sentences over 45 words.

description: Latin vocabulary and Latin case-name formulae persist untranslated in legal writing.
evidence: Names of writs (mandamus, certiorari) and terminology for case names (versus, ex rel., etc.) are still in Latin, perhaps a reflection of the use of Latin for writs and court records until the early 18th century.
testable: Match a Latin lexicon plus the case-name pattern \b[A-Z][a-z]+ v\. [A-Z][a-z]+ and count occurrences per document.

description: Everyday legal nouns descend from Anglo-Norman Law French and form a closed core vocabulary that general English does not use.
evidence: In legal pleadings, Anglo-Norman developed into Law French, from which many words in modern legal English are derived. These include property, estate, chattel, lease, executor, and tenant.
testable: Score the share of tokens drawn from a Law French term list, including -or/-ee pairs and -age endings.

description: Technical vocabulary peculiar to law that a lay reader cannot decode from ordinary meaning.
evidence: Legal English, in common with the language used by other trades and professions, employs a great deal of technical terminology which is unfamiliar to the layman (e.g. waiver, restraint of trade, restrictive covenant, promissory estoppel).
testable: Match a domain lexicon of multi-word terms of art and report density per 1000 words against a general-English baseline.

description: Common English words are redefined inside law and mean something different from their everyday sense.
evidence: These terms of art include ordinary words used with special meanings.
testable: Flag high-frequency everyday words from a legal-sense list when they appear in a contract or statute context rather than in narrative prose.

description: A defined word or phrase is written with initial capitals every time it recurs, turning capitalisation into a grammatical signal.
evidence: Make sure all instances of a defined term use initial capitals.
testable: Find definitions (X means, X has the meaning given in) then count mid-sentence capitalised noun phrases that repeat that head noun.

description: Text points at other provisions and at external authority by number and abbreviation instead of restating them.
evidence: Statutes are divided into parts, sections, subsections, paragraphs and subparagraphs.
testable: Count patterns of (section|s|clause|paragraph|schedule|Article|pt) plus a number, and reporter patterns such as \d+ U\.S\. \d+.

description: Citations add a page pinpoint after the first page so the reader lands on the exact passage relied on.
evidence: The reference to page 480 is referred to as a "pincite" or "pinpoint."
testable: Detect a reporter citation followed by a second page number and comma, then count such pincites per 1000 words.

description: Exceptions and conditions are tacked on with provided that, save that or subject to instead of being written as separate sentences.
evidence: So I disagree with Ben on all counts: First, the traditional trappings that often accompany provisos are archaic.
testable: Count proviso introducers per sentence and flag sentences containing two or more (provided that plus however), which signals bolted-on modules.

description: Verbs such as agree, grant and warrant do the legal act by being uttered, typically in the present tense with hereby.
evidence: One can identify a performative verb by using the hereby test.
testable: Count present-tense verbs with a party subject that sit next to hereby, using the hereby test as the criterion.

description: Legal style avoids first and second person, so obligations are stated about third-person roles rather than about I or you.
evidence: A related characteristic of legal style is impersonal constructions.
testable: Count I, we and you per 1000 words; a near-zero rate with third-person role subjects indicates impersonality.

description: The same noun is repeated where ordinary English would use a pronoun, to remove any chance of ambiguous reference.
evidence: One means of gaining precision is to repeat nouns (e.g., player), rather than using a pronoun (e.g., he) after a person or thing is introduced.
testable: Measure the ratio of repeated definite noun phrases to third-person pronouns within a document; high repetition with few pronouns marks the feature.

description: Drafting declares the masculine to include the feminine, or uses generic he, instead of gender-neutral wording.
evidence: Legal documents often declare that the masculine includes the feminine, the singular includes the plural, or that one tense includes the other.
testable: Count generic he/his/him and the clause the masculine includes the feminine or he or she per 1000 words.

description: The said, such and the same are used as adjectives pointing back at a noun already named, so the words double as articles.
evidence: The use of the terms often do not replace the noun but are used as adjectives to modify the noun.
testable: Count the said, such, the same and the aforementioned immediately before a noun, and such with no preceding as.

description: Adverbs and complements are placed after the noun they modify, splitting subjects from verbs in ways ordinary English forbids.
evidence: For example, the provisions for termination hereinafter appearing or will at the cost of the borrower forthwith comply with the same.
examples: the provisions for termination hereinafter appearing
testable: Flag post-modified nouns with hereinafter/aforesaid after the head noun, and sentences whose subject and finite verb are more than eight words apart.

description: Reciprocal roles are marked by -er/-or for the actor and -ee for the party acted upon.
evidence: Legal English contains some words and titles, such as employer and employee; lessor and lessee, in which the reciprocal and opposite nature of the relationship is indicated by the use of alternative endings.
testable: Count -ee nouns whose -er/-or counterpart also appears in the document, which marks a two-party instrument.

description: Multi-word verbs take a quasi-technical legal sense that differs from the everyday verb.
evidence: Phrasal verbs play a large role in legal English and are often used in a quasi-technical sense, such as parties enter into contracts, put down deposits, serve [documents] upon other parties, write off debts, attend at locations, and so on.
testable: Match a list of phrasal verbs in legal senses (enter into a contract, serve upon, attend at) and count them per 1000 words.

description: Prohibitions are written as negations, often several to a clause, rather than as positive statements.
evidence: Legal language seems to use an inordinate amount of negation.
testable: Count not, no, never, unless and except per sentence and flag clauses carrying more than one negator.

description: A prepositional phrase replaces a single adverb or preposition, adding bulk without adding meaning.
evidence: Lawyers also tend to use ponderous phrases (such as at slow speed or subsequent to) where a single word would suffice (slowly; after).
testable: Match a list (prior to, subsequent to, in the event of, in accordance with, with respect to) and count against single-word equivalents (before, after, if, under).
